title: Li Zhi, the Singer Who Never Holds His Tongue, on His Running Fight With “Commercialization”
excerpt: For an independent singer, commercialization is always a source of inner conflict.
body:
For an independent singer, commercialization is always a source of inner conflict.

On April 15, in Beijing, Li Zhi held a press conference for his upcoming “arena-scale” tour, Li Zhi “See” 2015 Concert Tour. Six arena shows in six cities in quick succession: Shenzhen on May 23, Xi’an on May 29, Shanghai on June 6, Wuhan on June 13, Chongqing on June 20 and Beijing on June 27. It is the first time an independent musician’s own team has launched and run a tour like this, for Li Zhi and for the “independent music scene” alike.

To promote what Li Zhi calls this “big, loud” run of shows, he appeared at the press conference, gave a string of interviews and sat for magazine photo shoots in a studio. People who know how Li Zhi usually operates call it “unprecedented,” or a “slap in the face.” He sums it up himself: “Losing face today is how I get to hold my head high tomorrow.”

Li Zhi says, “This is my job,” and “I have an obligation to cooperate.” But more often he says, “I don’t care,” and “I don’t think about these things.” Either way, he has every line covered.

For the tour, Li Zhi and his team rehearse six days a week, have reworked the band’s lineup and have made every part of the operation more precise. After the six shows, Li Zhi will go back to playing livehouses. So the tour, as he puts it, sounds grandiose but has a basic purpose: “to improve my own abilities.” There is one more reason: “I want to invite my parents to Workers’ Stadium to see a show, so they can stop worrying.”

At the i/O New Year’s Eve show in 2014, Li Zhi sold 3,600 tickets in 13 minutes. Of all the New Year’s Eve shows he has put on since 2010, it was the best “business” he had done: he lost only 10,000 yuan. The company as a whole has never turned a profit. But you cannot say this “one-man music business” has failed: for 10 years it has kept running, and it can borrow money whenever it needs to. Li Zhi thinks it is all fine, and believes “there will be big money later. When you do things well, it comes naturally.”

![Li Zhi](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702144757b6uLNxE92MWVZjI1.jpg-w600)Copyright is one example. Li Zhi left Xiami, then came back to Xiami three or four years later, and in between his income from digital licensing went from almost nothing to several hundred thousand yuan a year. That is one sum of “money that comes naturally when you do things well.”

But Li Zhi says copyright is fundamentally not about money. It is about rights: “I feel I own my work. That right matters more than the copyright itself. I can give it to you, but you can’t just take it.”

He says the quality he values most is honesty, and he says sincerely, “I don’t need people to like my music. My musical talent is quite ordinary. But I hope people like my values.” Most of those values show up in his foul-mouthed posts on Weibo. Set aside the argument over his manner, though, and you have to admit there is little in those values to “dislike.” At bottom, they are universal things like equality and kindness.

### “I’m treating this as an affair. This time I’m shameless.”

![Li Zhi](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702144757kanQL0XTMCIOYcdH.jpg-w600)In 2007, at a music festival, Li Zhi talked for a long time with a female reporter. At the end she asked him, “Are you Zhou Yunpeng?” After that, he stopped giving interviews.

The story has circulated widely. Asked to confirm it, Li Zhi says it is part of the reason; the other part is that he “doesn’t much like the media.” But however much he dislikes it, Li Zhi is carrying out his “obligation” for the coming tour.

QDaily: You’ve started giving interviews for this tour. That’s a change, in a way.

Li Zhi: It’s not a change. I think about it quite simply. Frankly, I don’t expect any interview to help the media understand me, or to portray me in a fairly positive light. And sometimes I don’t care. All my cooperation is just to keep up some buzz. Put another way, I feel I should do my part of the work now, and interviews are one part of my work.

QDaily: Why weren’t interviews your work before?

Li Zhi: Because none of my earlier shows needed this much noise.

QDaily: Is the noise this time because you face pressure over ticket sales?

Li Zhi: No. In terms of publicity, interviews don’t do much for ticket sales, especially with my audience. It’s unlikely that a stranger who doesn’t know who Li Zhi is will see the publicity and go buy a ticket. The odds are very low. My audience is the same as for my earlier shows: I post one Weibo message or send one WeChat push and they come. They’re used to that. However hard you push, other people won’t come.

So why do these press conferences and interviews at all? It’s just to make the event look bigger. I don’t care about that, but my partners do, so I have an obligation to cooperate.

QDaily: This is six concerts in a row, which no independent musician has done before. Do you worry that by one of the later shows, everyone who was going to come has already come, and the last one or two might have no audience? What then?

Li Zhi: I have thought about it, but it doesn’t matter. By my estimate, I suggested to them keeping each show at around 3,000 people, an arena-scale level. They have their own considerations. They figure 3,000 people and 5,000 people cost about the same, so they went bigger.

What you describe could happen, but it makes little difference to me. First, my earnings have nothing to do with ticket sales. I handle the performance and they take care of everything else. At bottom that is a question of face, and I don’t think about it. What I’m doing now is also to help them save face.

QDaily: Do you really not care?

Li Zhi: Do you think I’m someone who cares about image? Not caring means I won’t be happy about good press or hurt by bad press. I’ll take in all kinds of opinions.

![Li Zhi](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702144758GFTceRapO7tdUzsW.jpg-w600)

QDaily: You have always stressed that, apart from Luo Dayou and Cui Jian, you give no complimentary tickets. What if the organizers hand out comps on your behalf this time?

Li Zhi: Everything in this show that goes against my earlier principles and values, I accept. I’m treating this one as an affair. I figure this time I’m shameless, and I’m slapping my own face. That’s fine. I’ve thought it through: if I didn’t agree to do it this way, this show couldn’t go ahead.

QDaily: Some people ask, are you still Li Zhi like this?

Li Zhi: Yes, I am. Li Zhi isn’t someone who… always holds fast to one thing. He’s someone who keeps thinking. And I’ve thought it through: it’s an affair, not a divorce. I’ll come back.

Of course, if this experience convinces me that the way I did many things before was wrong, I’ll change it too. I won’t consider public opinion. Wrong is wrong.

### “What the masses demand is our greatest suffering”

![Li Zhi](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702144758VaSoKFdHNUficn98.jpg-w600)

Going from livehouses to arenas is of course more than a change in stage size. Li Zhi and his team have prepared a great deal for it, including rehearsing six days a week.

He says he is pushing himself hard, and gives the most basic reason: “First, the purpose of this show is to improve my own abilities, including those of our band and team. That’s the first reason. The second is that from the time I started making music until now, I have done it for myself.”

QDaily: You played Workers’ Stadium last year, but it was a multi-act bill. This time you carry a whole show alone. What extra preparation does that take?

Li Zhi: A great deal. Each scale demands its own level of ability. It looks like you’re just stepping onto a stage, but singing 10 songs versus singing for one or two hours, and two hours versus three hours, are completely different things. Everything is about the same in principle, but once the volume goes up, you find it very hard to coordinate. One dinner engagement a day doesn’t tire you out. Ten dinner engagements in a day do. That’s roughly the idea.

QDaily: Specifically, has the band’s lineup changed?

Li Zhi: Yes. We took out the horns and violin from the New Year’s Eve show, and added a harmonica.

QDaily: It sounds like it’s become simpler.

Li Zhi: Yes, because first of all, the number of songs won’t be like the New Year’s Eve show, which had no set plan. At the longest we played six or seven hours. This time it’ll be held to under two and a half hours, so there will certainly be fewer songs.

From the outside, you’d think there are fewer songs and not much change in the arrangements, but in fact I’m working on the fine details. When you go to a livehouse show, a changeover between two bands of 10 minutes or half an hour is normal. So how do we get it down to two minutes, or one? The workload is enormous. In the same way, the transition between two songs I sing, whether 10 seconds, a minute or two seconds, makes for completely different demands. Since we started rehearsing on March 1, everything we’ve done has been about getting more precise. We now rehearse six days a week, about four hours a day.

QDaily: That’s a demand you place on yourself. Listeners may not care.

Li Zhi: Right. So this goes to the main purpose of doing this show. To do a standard so-called concert at this scale (I used to prefer calling them shows or recitals), the people in every link have to improve a lot to get that result. A gap in any one link lowers the quality of your show.

QDaily: But what is this experience for? Afterward you’ll go back to playing livehouses.

Li Zhi: Once your ability improves, you’ll be different in livehouses too.

### “At least up to now, all these years, it can still run. It just hasn’t made big money.”

Li Zhi sums up his complicated identity as both independent musician and businessman as a “one-man music business.” As the company’s legal representative, he describes his role this way: “I actually manage nothing, and I also manage everything.” So far, this boss’s books are still in the red. But Li Zhi believes “there will be big money later. When you do things well, it comes naturally.”

QDaily: You didn’t insist on being a “one-man business” from the moment you started treating this as work, did you? I know both Thirteenth Month and Universal planned to sign you, and talks were mostly done. Why did you hit the brakes?

Li Zhi: My thinking back then was really narrow. I just thought, what do I get out of signing with you? Anything you can do I can do myself, and what you do might be something I don’t like. Sometimes I even felt I could do it better than they could, though I was only one person and you were record labels. But now I don’t think that way. As I see it, what is this “independent music” crap? It’s all cooperation.

QDaily: Because you need a team too.

Li Zhi: Right. In essence it’s also a record label, except I’m my own boss, and others don’t decide what I do. I’m used to freedom.

QDaily: Deciding everything yourself has real drawbacks.

Li Zhi: It gets narrow.

QDaily: Has your company turned a profit on its books?

Li Zhi: No.

QDaily: Then what do you do? Everyone depends on you for a living.

Li Zhi: So my debts keep growing. Take it slowly, it doesn’t matter. It can still run. It just hasn’t made big money.

QDaily: So are you doing it just for fun?

Li Zhi: Not that either. I think there will be big money later. When you do things well, it comes naturally.

QDaily: Where do you think the big money will come from?

Li Zhi: The performances themselves.

QDaily: Would you do commercial shows?

Li Zhi: It depends. If you asked me to endorse a sanitary pad, of course I couldn’t. Music festivals count as commercial shows, so I can take part. A real estate developer’s launch event, I’d look at which developer. Someone like Vanke would be fine.

QDaily: You’re also developing some merchandise now. Is that a way of pleasing your audience?

Li Zhi: No. I make merchandise to gain experience. Grandiose again, right? Really it’s that I’m always preparing to quit this line of work. I won’t start an IT company, I won’t make apps, I won’t make phones. I might make a bottle of water, or a piece of clothing, something solid and physical.

QDaily: You say you’re in debt now, and you plan to keep making music, yet you’re always ready to stop. Isn’t that contradictory?

Li Zhi: Not contradictory. Our revenue looks quite large, but the profit is very, very small. I think that’s fine; we’re always investing. Like our New Year’s Eve shows, we kept losing money, 200,000, 300,000, 500,000. So we lose it. Then suddenly one year, like last year, we lost only 10,000. How good is that? That’s one way of thinking.

The second way of thinking: I’m always ready for the day when no one comes to my shows anymore. Then what? It’s not in my nature to hang around shamelessly.

QDaily: Looking back, if you hadn’t been as narrow-minded as you say, would you have signed with a label back then?

Li Zhi: Yes.

QDaily: Do you feel like you’re riding a tiger now, unable to get off?

Li Zhi: No. I think it’s pretty good now. I’m in control of everything.

QDaily: And you definitely won’t sign with a label in the future?

Li Zhi: Definitely not. I need to make some compromises, but I don’t need to compromise with record labels. I pick my own people, and if the cooperation isn’t good, I switch. I know there are many things I can’t decide, I don’t have the ability to do them, but at least I can decide whether to do something or not.![Li Zhi](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702144759QVrKjF01POZEibR5.jpg-w600)

QDaily: Does joining a label make you feel you’d have no competitive edge?

Li Zhi: A label has only a handful of people, with hundreds of artists under it. Who is going to help you? Even if they’re willing, they don’t have the energy to really look after you.

### “I can give it to you, but you can’t just take it.”

Any talk of Li Zhi eventually runs into copyright. In 2010 he walked out of Xiami and demanded that the various music platforms take down his unauthorized works. Then last year, Li Zhi’s new album *1701* debuted on Xiami, with a license signed and a handshake to make peace. Talks with other platforms are under way, one after another.

On copyright, Li Zhi says it is not about money, but “I feel I own my work. That right matters more than the copyright itself. I can give it to you, but you can’t just take it.”

QDaily: When did you first use the internet?

Li Zhi: 1999.

QDaily: To do what?

Li Zhi: Back then it was BBS, forums.

QDaily: Did you also download pirated music?

Li Zhi: I did.

QDaily: You did this yourself, and now you ask others not to pirate. Do you have the standing to?

Li Zhi: I think everyone goes through a stupid stage, everyone goes through an ignorant stage. That’s nothing to be ashamed of. It’s an inevitable part of growing up. No one is born with everything clear and orderly. What matters is that you realize it’s wrong and work to change it.

A lot of the time you’re limited by your circumstances. When we used pirated software, spending several thousand yuan on an operating system was out of the question. Now that I have money, naturally I don’t use pirated copies. In my value system, the meaning of a person’s life is to keep correcting your own mistakes.

QDaily: On piracy, you may be a beneficiary. For example, you got access to some good music earlier by downloading pirated copies, then went on to make music yourself, and your own music first spread through piracy too.

Li Zhi: I got a lot of information through pirated channels, that’s true, and I’m making up for it now by paying for those artists’ concerts. The second part I don’t accept. From the start, essentially, I wasn’t pushing that spread. Even two years ago, I opposed their promoting my work so more people could hear it. So that was meaningless to me. It may have meaning in your eyes, but it wasn’t part of my motive.

QDaily: A passive benefit is still a benefit.

Li Zhi: You’re right to say that, but if you put it that way, is the pleasure of rape the same as the pleasure of sex?

QDaily: The responsible party isn’t you.

Li Zhi: That’s why the saying matters: what God sees is not your actions but your will. Among humans it’s simple. We look at both motive and action. Put the two together and it’s even clearer in law: there is intentional killing and unintentional killing.

QDaily: You’ve also lived through the shift from physical records to digital copyright. You used to burn your CDs, and now you still release CDs. Are you split again?

Li Zhi: It’s not a split. Why did I burn them back then? First, I have a habit of burning things. I still regularly clear out things at home and take them out to burn. Second, they wouldn’t sell and made no money, and it hurt to look at them, so I burned them.

So why do I make them now? Because making records now takes no effort or money from me. I make the music myself, an mp3 or a WAV; that I have to do. After that, JD.com and others handle production, pressing and sales. I put in no manpower or money, yet they can still earn me a bit, and all the risk is theirs. I just provide a master tape. I have no costs.

QDaily: You’ve started chasing money.

Li Zhi: Inevitably. And I don’t think that’s a bad thing. Who doesn’t?

QDaily: Copyright has really been going through destruction and rebuilding, and is now moving toward monopoly.

Li Zhi: I’m not very clear on how the copyright industry has developed. I don’t much care. What I care about is that my things are mine. Whether I’m happy to sell or not is none of your business.

QDaily: One could read that as a freedom only someone who already benefits can enjoy.

Li Zhi: I don’t think the people who give their work away free are idiots. That’s a way and a route that suits them. But for me it’s different. At least in the first five years, I had no motive to spread my work. Second, I feel I own my work, and that matters more than the copyright itself. I can give it to you, but you can’t just take it.

QDaily: With digital copyright in the picture, there are actually more links in the chain. Does it feel more chaotic to you?

Li Zhi: For me it’s a good thing. I think digital music displacing CDs is scientific progress, just as CDs displaced cassette tapes. It’s progress. But that’s secondary. What matters is that however things get displaced, the rights you hold over your own work are the core.

### “First, is it reliable. Then comes the money.”

It would not be accurate to call this tour strictly a “one-man fight” either. Besides Li Zhi’s own Free Fall, the partners listed on the poster include S.A.G (Beijing Bosheng Brothers Culture Communication), Letong and LeTV.

Being free to choose partners is one of the main reasons Li Zhi chose to be a “one-man business,” and his rule is: “First look at whether they’re reliable, then the money.”

QDaily: For this concert you chose to work with S.A.G, Letong and LeTV. Does this signal a tilt toward working with the internet?

Li Zhi: The internet is just one way, just a tool. Choosing a car or a train, we only look at effect and efficiency. Of course that’s also empty talk. First is whether they’re reliable, then comes the money. Because I can’t tolerate unreliable people and companies.

QDaily: You’ve worked with LeTV before on a livestream of a concert. What do you think of that format?

Li Zhi: I think it’s pretty good. After all, many people don’t have time to go to the live show.

QDaily: Do you think it will become a trend?

Li Zhi: Honestly, I’m not very optimistic. Every ball game is very different, and the audience is very broad. But music like ours, if you do a lot of it, it’s all about the same. Take Eason Chan’s 20-show world tour. How much difference is there from show to show?

### “What am I selling? Attitude, I suppose. Hard work, honesty.”

Li Zhi likes Luo Yonghao, and makes no secret of it, because more than 99 percent of what Luo says is the truth.

But as we fell into small talk at the end, Li Zhi added one more line: “If honesty were a virtue, the world would fall into chaos.”

QDaily: You’ve said Li Zhi surely isn’t selling his voice, and selling his looks doesn’t seem workable either. Are you selling sentiment?

Li Zhi: What I sell is attitude, I suppose. Hard work, honesty.

QDaily: That could produce a gap. You think that’s what you’re selling, but the audience feels that’s not what they bought.

Li Zhi: No problem. What you use this cucumber for is none of my business. Ideally, of course, you eat it. Take Luo Yonghao making phones: he isn’t making them so you can take them out and raffle them off, right? Can he control that?

QDaily: You seem to agree with Luo Yonghao a lot.

Li Zhi: I often say about Luo Yonghao that China may not need Smartisan phones, but humanity, or at least China, badly needs people like Luo Yonghao.

QDaily: Needs what about him?

Li Zhi: The whole person. His ways and methods, not that all of them are right, but they make sense. What he says is the truth. But do you know how many people in this industry tell the truth? How many people in China tell the truth? Especially you guys… no, I have to cooperate with the interview.
